name.text: 01 Question: Four Canonical Classes of Textual Variation

questiontext.text: <p>Which four fundamental categories encompass all textual divergences identified during manuscript collation?</p>

answer.text: <p>Substitution, addition, omission, and transposition.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Textual criticism classifies all textual variance into substitutions (replacements), additions (insertions), omissions (deletions), and transpositions (word-order inversions).</p>

answer.text: <p>Compression, encryption, decryption, and decompression.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are computer science data transmission terms, not philological variant categories.</p>

answer.text: <p>Paleography, codicology, epigraphy, and papyrology.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are auxiliary historical disciplines, not textual variant classes.</p>

answer.text: <p>Parchment, papyrus, paper, and vellum.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. These are physical manuscript writing materials.</p>

name.text: 02 Question: Role of the Base Text in Collation

questiontext.text: <p>Why is a 'base text' (or *textus collatus*) conventionally chosen when conducting textual collation?</p>

answer.text: <p>It provides a constant reference point against which all witness divergences and coordinates can be systematically recorded and indexed.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. A base text serves as a stable coordinate system and comparison standard, even if the editor does not believe it represents the original text.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because the base text is legally required to be the oldest manuscript surviving in the world.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Base texts are chosen for editorial convenience or accessibility, not necessarily age.</p>

answer.text: <p>To ensure that no other manuscripts are allowed to disagree with it.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. The entire point of collation is to discover and record where witnesses disagree with the base text.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because computer algorithms cannot function without declaring one manuscript as divine truth.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Algorithmic collation is neutral; the base text merely anchors string alignment.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>How do biological sequence alignment algorithms like Needleman-Wunsch and Gotoh apply to automated textual collation?</p>

answer.text: <p>They use dynamic programming matrix calculation to find the optimal global alignment of character or token sequences while penalizing gaps and mismatches.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Needleman-Wunsch and Gotoh compute optimal alignments between textual strings by minimizing cost functions for insertions, deletions, and substitutions.</p>

answer.text: <p>They automatically reconstruct the exact handwriting speed of the ancient scribe.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Alignment algorithms evaluate string distances, not scribal physical biomechanics.</p>

answer.text: <p>They convert Greek and Latin words into DNA nucleotide base pairs (A, C, G, T) to test biological tissue origin.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Although originally developed for bioinformatics, textual critics apply the mathematical logic of the algorithms to linguistic tokens.</p>

answer.text: <p>They force all sentences in different languages to have the identical number of words.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Alignment algorithms allow gaps (insertions/deletions) to accommodate differing sentence lengths.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why is the choice of tokenization method critical when feeding witness transcriptions into the CollateX engine?</p>

answer.text: <p>Word-level tokenization aligns substantive lexical units, whereas character-level tokenization aligns individual letters and can obscure word-boundary shifts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Tokenization determines the atomic unit of comparison: word-level matches semantic units, while character-level catches intra-word spelling variations.</p>

answer.text: <p>CollateX cannot process text unless every single word is exactly five letters long.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CollateX handles arbitrary token lengths seamlessly.</p>

answer.text: <p>Tokenization is only required if the input files are saved as binary executable files.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Tokenization is the essential first step of parsing plain text into a sequence of linguistic symbols.</p>

answer.text: <p>Character-level tokenization deletes all vowels automatically from the source text.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Character tokenization preserves all characters while breaking them into discrete sequence elements.</p>

name.text: 05 Question: Topology of a Variant Graph

questiontext.text: <p>In CollateX, how is a textual tradition visually and topologically represented?</p>

answer.text: <p>As a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) where nodes represent tokens and edges represent the sequential paths taken by different manuscript witnesses.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. A variant graph models textual variation as a DAG: shared readings converge on single nodes, while variant readings branch into parallel paths before rejoining.</p>

answer.text: <p>As a concentric circular pie chart showing the weight of parchment.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Variant graphs are topological network graphs, not pie charts.</p>

answer.text: <p>As a 3D polygonal terrain map indicating elevation changes.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CollateX outputs directed graphs and tables, not topographical maps.</p>

answer.text: <p>As an unlinked scatterplot where words are placed randomly across a coordinate grid.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Nodes in a variant graph are strictly connected by directional sequence edges representing witness readings.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Which TEI element structure correctly represents a point of textual variation among multiple manuscript witnesses in a parallel segmentation apparatus?</p>

answer.text: <p><app><lem wit="#witA">reading_A</lem><rdg wit="#witB">reading_B</rdg></app></p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. In TEI parallel segmentation, <app> encloses the variant location, with <lem> holding the base/preferred lemma and <rdg> holding variant witness readings.</p>

answer.text: <p><choice><sic>reading_A</sic><corr>reading_B</corr></choice></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <sic> and <corr> represent scribal errors and editorial corrections in a single witness, not collation variants across multiple witnesses.</p>

answer.text: <p><subst><del>reading_A</del><add>reading_B</add></subst></p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. <subst> represents physical alterations on a single manuscript folio.</p>

answer.text: <p><milestone unit="variant"/>reading_A//reading_B</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Milestones are empty boundary markers, not container elements for critical apparatus data.</p>

name.text: 07 Question: Transposition Challenge in Linear Alignment

questiontext.text: <p>Why do standard dynamic programming collation algorithms struggle when two witnesses exhibit a word-order transposition (e.g. 'Christ Jesus' vs 'Jesus Christ')?</p>

answer.text: <p>Because linear alignment algorithms assume monotonic sequence progression and typically interpret a transposition as an omission in one place coupled with an addition elsewhere.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Dynamic programming optimizes monotonic sequence alignment; recognizing that a displaced word is the same lexical item moved across another requires non-linear transposition detection heuristics.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because XML schemas forbid the rearrangement of words under any circumstances.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. XML schemas validate markup structure, not textual word order.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because the algorithm automatically deletes both words to resolve the paradox.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CollateX does not delete data; it represents it as an alignment gap or parallel branch.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because transpositions only exist in modern printed novels, never in handwritten manuscripts.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Transposition (metathesis) is one of the most common scribal phenomena in manuscript traditions.</p>

name.text: 08 Question: Stemmatic Value of Conjunctive Errors

questiontext.text: <p>In classical Lachmannian stemmatology, what is a 'conjunctive error' (*error coniunctivus*) and why is it essential?</p>

answer.text: <p>A shared distinctive error that is so improbable to have occurred independently by coincidence that it proves the witnesses sharing it descend from a common ancestor.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Conjunctive errors establish genealogical kinship between witnesses because two independent scribes would not spontaneously commit the identical idiosyncratic mistake.</p>

answer.text: <p>A spelling error in a conjunction such as 'and' or 'but'.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Conjunctive errors refer to genealogical connection (*coniungere*), not parts of speech.</p>

answer.text: <p>A syntax error caused by connecting an external hard drive during collation.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Conjunctive error is a fundamental philological concept in textual stemmatics.</p>

answer.text: <p>An error that occurs when two lines of text physically overlap on a palimpsest.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. That is a codicological/optical phenomenon, not a genealogical conjunctive error.</p>

name.text: 09 Question: Semantic vs Orthographic Variation in AI Auditing

questiontext.text: <p>When using an LLM to categorize variant readings extracted by CollateX, what critical boundary must the prompt instruct the model to observe?</p>

answer.text: <p>The model must strictly separate orthographic/phonetic variants from substantive semantic variants that affect syntax, lexicon, or theological/historical interpretation.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. LLMs must be explicitly constrained to distinguish superficial phonetic noise from substantive readings that carry stemmatic and semantic weight.</p>

answer.text: <p>The model must rewrite all variants in modern French.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Historical collation must preserve the original languages of the witnesses.</p>

answer.text: <p>The model must assume that the witness with the best handwriting is automatically the author's original.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Calligraphic elegance does not correlate with textual authenticity.</p>

answer.text: <p>The model must discard any variant that contains more than two syllables.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Syllable count is irrelevant to variant validity.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why can automated tools like CollateX never fully replace the human scholarly editor in establishing a critical text?</p>

answer.text: <p>Because software can align strings and calculate mathematical edit distances, but only human scholars can evaluate paleographical plausibility, scribal psychology, dialectal nuance, and historical context.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Computational collation automates the mechanical identification of divergence; the critical evaluation of causes and the establishment of the text remains an interpretive scholarly act.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because computer processors cannot store non-English alphabets in their internal memory.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Unicode enables modern computers to handle virtually all historical scripts.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because publishing houses refuse to print books unless every single word was typed without software assistance.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Academic publishers actively embrace digital scholarly methods.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because collation algorithms always crash if more than three manuscripts are compared at once.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CollateX routinely collates dozens of manuscript witnesses simultaneously.</p>
